halo-laser-hybrid-fractional.summary: A clinic laser that treats two skin depths in one pass to even out tone and smooth scars and texture, with small registered studies behind it.

quick.overview:
Halo is a hybrid fractional laser that combines two wavelengths in a single treatment. People use it to get a more even skin tone and smoother texture, and to soften sun damage, pigment and scars.

It works by creating microscopic columns of controlled injury, one set shallow and one deeper, which the skin heals by remodeling. Registered studies are small: a 15-person study of facial and neck photoaging, a 34-person study of conditions including dyschromia and photodamage, and a trial of a hybrid fractional laser for acne scars in skin of color.
quick.how: Halo is done in a dermatology or aesthetic clinic, usually as a single session or a short series. Downtime depends on how deep the settings are set, so people plan recovery around the chosen intensity. Results build as skin remodels over the following weeks.
quick.risks: Hyperpigmentation after laser treatment is a studied concern, particularly in darker skin tones. Redness, swelling and peeling occur while skin heals, and downtime varies with settings. It is a clinic-only procedure, and people with active skin infections or a tendency to scar should raise that with the provider.

angle.text: Halo combines ablative and non-ablative wavelengths in one pass so skin resurfaces at two depths and remodels, evening tone and smoothing scars and texture. People use it for sun damage, scars and pigment, and registered studies of 15 to 34 people have examined it.

fractional-co2-laser-co2re-ultrapulse-sm.summary: The strongest fractional laser resurfacing option, used to smooth scars and deep wrinkles through deep collagen remodeling, with a longer recovery than gentler lasers.

quick.overview:
Fractional CO2 is the heavy-duty option in laser resurfacing, used to smooth acne and surgical scars and soften deep wrinkles and photodamage. CO2RE, UltraPulse and SmartXide are common systems.

The 10,600 nm beam is absorbed by water in the skin and vaporizes microscopic columns of tissue, with untreated skin between them speeding healing. The skin then rebuilds collagen over the following months. It is among the better-studied fractional lasers, with burn-scar cohorts, acne scar studies in Asian patients and randomized trials combined with other therapies.
quick.how: It is performed in a clinic, often with numbing, and is usually a single session or a small series rather than a frequent routine. People plan a recovery period with redness, swelling and peeling, which is typically longer than after non-ablative lasers. Final results are judged after healing and continued collagen remodeling.
quick.risks: Reported risks include hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation, scarring, acne and herpes outbreaks. Wikipedia notes CO2 resurfacing carries higher risk of pigment loss and scarring than erbium lasers. Recovery is longer than for gentler lasers, and darker skin tones and people with a history of cold sores or poor healing should discuss this with the provider.

angle.text: Fractional CO2 vaporizes microscopic columns of skin, and deep collagen remodeling follows, smoothing scars and deep wrinkles over a longer recovery. It is the more intensive fractional laser and has the larger research base, including randomized trials.

erbium-yag-resurfacing.summary: A shallower, water-targeting resurfacing laser that peels thin skin layers with less heat than CO2 to smooth texture, scars and wrinkles.

quick.overview:
Er:YAG resurfacing removes thin layers of skin to smooth acne scars, deep wrinkles and pigment such as melasma. It is described as a gentler-heat alternative to CO2.

The 2940 nm beam is strongly absorbed by water and ablates shallow layers with limited heat spreading into surrounding tissue. Wikipedia says this gives a lower risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than CO2. Much of the early Er:YAG research concerns dental tissue; skin trials in the sources are small registrations covering skin aging, acne scars with PRP and cutaneous neurofibromas.
quick.how: It is done in a clinic, in one session or a short series depending on the depth wanted. Skin typically looks pink and peels while it heals, with a recovery that depends on settings. It is sometimes combined with other treatments for acne scars.
quick.risks: Reported risks of laser resurfacing include scarring, pigment change, acne and herpes outbreaks. Redness, swelling and peeling are expected during healing. People prone to cold sores, scarring or pigment changes should discuss this with the provider.

angle.text: Er:YAG removes thin layers of skin with a water-absorbing laser, so skin heals with less heat damage and ends up smoother, with fewer scars and wrinkles. It is used for acne scars, deep wrinkles and melasma, and is described as shallower than CO2.

pico-genesis-picosure-pro.summary: Picosecond laser treatments that break up pigment and soften acne scars and texture, with short downtime and small published studies so far.

quick.overview:
PicoSure Pro is a 755 nm picosecond alexandrite laser that clinics use for acne scars, pigmented spots, wrinkles and tattoo work, aiming for clearer tone and softer scars. "Pico Genesis" appears on forums and clinic menus as a name for picosecond-style skin treatments.

Picosecond pulses deliver energy in trillionths of a second, which proponents describe as a mainly photomechanical effect that shatters pigment rather than relying on heat. A diffractive lens array can add small zones of skin change for scars and texture. A 2025 prospective single-center study combined it with radiofrequency microneedling for atrophic acne scars, and a 23-person post-market trial was registered.
quick.how: It is performed in a clinic, usually as a series of sessions spaced weeks apart. Many people choose it for the short recovery. Pigment and tone changes build over a few sessions, and it is sometimes paired with other scar treatments such as RF microneedling.
quick.risks: Short-lived redness and swelling are generally described. Pigment changes are a recognised concern with laser treatments of skin, especially in darker skin types. Long-term comparative data are scarce, and the results reported vary by device and condition.

angle.text: Picosecond pulses break up pigment and stimulate skin remodeling with short downtime, leaving clearer tone and softer scars. PicoSure Pro is used for acne scars, pigmented spots and skin texture, and published studies are small.

ruby-laser.summary: The first laser ever built, used historically for hair removal, pigment spots and tattoos; newer wavelengths have largely replaced it for hair.

quick.overview:
The ruby laser emits deep-red light at 694.3 nm. Theodore Maiman built it in 1960 as the first working laser, and it was among the first used in medicine, for tattoos and, from the 1990s, hair removal.

Ruby light is absorbed by melanin, so dark hair follicles and pigment spots heat up selectively, giving fewer dark hairs and lighter pigment. Studies in the 1990s reported follicle damage and hair reduction, and registered trials examined Q-switched ruby for sun-related pigment spots (lentigines). Wikipedia states alexandrite and Nd:YAG lasers have largely replaced ruby for hair removal.
quick.how: Today it is mostly a historical technology, and clinics typically offer newer wavelengths for hair removal. Hair removal with ruby used pulses in the hundreds of microseconds to milliseconds over repeated sessions, while Q-switched ruby uses nanosecond pulses for pigment and ink.
quick.risks: Because melanin in skin also absorbs 694 nm light, pigment changes and burns are recognised risks, especially in darker skin. Wikipedia lists ruby among lasers suited to paler skin types for hair removal.

angle.text: Ruby light is absorbed by melanin, so hair follicles or pigment spots are heated and the result is fewer dark hairs and lighter pigment. It is the first laser ever built and is now largely replaced by alexandrite and Nd:YAG for hair removal.

alexandrite-laser-hair-removal.summary: A 755 nm clinic laser that reduces dark facial and body hair, mainly on lighter skin, across a series of sessions.

quick.overview:
Alexandrite lasers reduce dark facial and body hair, and clinics commonly use them for fast treatment of large areas on lighter skin tones. The result is visibly less hair growth, a reduction rather than guaranteed total removal.

The 755 nm light is strongly absorbed by melanin, so it heats the hair and follicle while skin cooling protects the surface, damaging actively growing follicles. Alexandrite is among the more studied hair-removal lasers; Wikipedia describes a 2006 review that found roughly 67 to 72 percent reduction at six months across alexandrite, diode and IPL.
quick.how: Treatment is done in a clinic over multiple sessions spaced weeks apart, because only actively growing hairs respond at any one time. It works best on dark, coarse hair; light, grey, red or fine hair responds poorly. Many people shave beforehand and then maintain with occasional touch-up sessions.
quick.risks: Reported effects include redness, swelling, acne flares, burns and hyper- or hypopigmentation. The FDA defines "permanent" reduction as long-term stable reduction, not guaranteed removal. Tanned or darker skin carries higher pigment-change risk, so patients typically avoid sun exposure around sessions.

angle.text: Alexandrite light at 755 nm is absorbed by hair melanin, heating and damaging follicles so dark hair grows back visibly thinner and sparser over sessions. It is used for facial and body hair on lighter skin, and the research base on hair reduction is broad.

diode-laser-hair-removal-lightsheer.summary: The common 800-810 nm clinic laser for reducing facial and body hair on pale to medium skin; LightSheer is a widely used brand with registered trials.

quick.overview:
Diode lasers are among the most common clinic hair-removal devices, used to reduce facial and body hair for smoother, less hairy skin. LightSheer is a widely used diode line, and its handpieces have registered clinical studies for hair reduction.

Near-infrared light around 800-810 nm is absorbed by melanin in the hair, heating the follicle while skin cooling protects the surface. Wikipedia describes a randomized trial in which diode laser reduced hair by 69.2 percent at 12 months versus 52.7 percent for IPL.
quick.how: Treatment is done in a clinic, with sessions repeated every few weeks since only growing follicles are affected. Hair is usually shaved beforehand, and people typically see hair growth slow over the series. It suits pale to medium skin with dark hair.
quick.risks: Short-term redness, swelling and pain are common, and burns and pigment changes are possible. A 2006 review described by Wikipedia reported side effects in 28.9 percent for diode versus 9.5 percent for alexandrite. Results are a reduction rather than guaranteed permanent removal.

angle.text: Diode light at 800-810 nm heats melanin in the follicle so hair growth slows over sessions, leaving skin smoother and less hairy. It is the common clinic option for pale to medium skin, and a randomized trial reported 69.2 percent hair reduction at 12 months.

nd-yag-laser-hair-removal.summary: The 1064 nm laser used to reduce hair on darker skin tones, penetrating deeper with less absorption by surface melanin.

quick.overview:
Nd:YAG is the hair-removal laser used for darker skin tones, reducing facial and body hair while limiting absorption in the surface melanin. Wikipedia lists the 1064 nm wavelength as the one for dark skin, and a 2022 prospective study said alexandrite and Nd:YAG are the most effective options in lighter and darker skin phototypes respectively.

The longer wavelength is absorbed less by skin pigment and penetrates deeper, so it heats hair-follicle melanin while sparing the surface better. Studies of fluence and histology in the early 2000s examined millisecond Nd:YAG lasers for hair removal.
quick.how: It is done in a clinic over repeated sessions spaced weeks apart, since lasers act on actively growing follicles. Fine or light hair usually needs more sessions. Some clinics use an "in motion" technique, which a 2022 study compared with the traditional approach.
quick.risks: Redness, swelling, pain, burns and pigment change are possible, as with other laser hair removal. Results are a reduction rather than guaranteed removal. The 1064 nm beam is invisible, so eye protection is used.

angle.text: The 1064 nm wavelength penetrates deeper and is absorbed less by surface pigment, so follicles are heated with less skin damage and hair is reduced on darker skin. It is the option people with darker skin tones turn to for facial and body hair.

soprano-ice-laser.summary: A hair-removal laser line marketed as more comfortable; the Platinum model combines three wavelengths, with one small study in darker skin.

quick.overview:
Soprano Ice is a hair-removal laser line from Alma Lasers, marketed as a more comfortable option. The Soprano Ice Platinum combines 755, 810 and 1064 nm wavelengths in one device to reduce facial and body hair across a range of skin types.

Like other hair-removal lasers, it targets melanin in hair follicles by selective photothermolysis, with cooling to protect the skin. A 2021 paper in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology reported on the Platinum for hair reduction in Fitzpatrick skin types IV to V.
quick.how: Treatment is done in a clinic over a series of sessions spaced weeks apart. Combining wavelengths is described as an approach to treat a range of skin types. Users and clinics promote it for lower discomfort, though specific comparisons with other devices were not found.
quick.risks: General laser hair-removal risks apply: redness, swelling, burns and pigment changes. Specific data on pain reduction versus other devices were not found. Results are a reduction in hair rather than guaranteed removal.

angle.text: Soprano Ice uses three wavelengths, 755, 810 and 1064 nm, to heat follicles so hair growth slows with lower discomfort, leaving smoother, less hairy skin. One 2021 study evaluated the Platinum model in skin types IV to V.

gentlemax-pro.summary: Candela's alexandrite plus Nd:YAG clinic laser, used mainly to reduce facial and body hair across skin tones.

quick.overview:
GentleMax Pro is a Candela clinic laser that combines two wavelengths, alexandrite (755 nm) and Nd:YAG (1064 nm). It is mainly used to reduce facial and body hair for cleaner, less hairy skin, and also lists pigmented and vascular lesions.

Light absorbed by melanin in the hair heats and damages the follicle. Alexandrite is used across skin types and Nd:YAG is generally used on darker skin, which is the reason for pairing both in one machine. Studies naming this device are mostly small clinical series and safety reports, including a retrospective review of use on children after ear reconstruction.
quick.how: It is a professional device used by dermatology and aesthetic practices, with treatment typically spread over many sessions. Clinics choose the setting that suits the person's skin and hair type. Light or fine hair responds poorly, and in looksmaxxing circles it comes up mainly for facial hair reduction.
quick.risks: Reported effects include redness, swelling, acne flares, colour changes, burns and, rarely, a delayed hives-like rash after alexandrite epilation. Outcomes depend on skin and hair type and the operator.

angle.text: GentleMax Pro uses alexandrite and Nd:YAG light to heat follicles so hair growth reduces over sessions, giving cleaner, less hairy facial and body skin across skin tones. Studies naming the device are small, alongside the broad hair-removal literature.

candela-laser.summary: Brand name for a family of clinic lasers for hair, pigment, vessels and tattoos; people choose the device that matches their concern.

quick.overview:
Candela makes aesthetic laser systems, and in looksmaxxing talk "Candela laser" stands for the clinic machines it sells, such as the GentleMax Pro and the PicoWay. People pick the device that matches the concern: hair, pigment, redness or tattoos.

Different systems use different wavelengths: alexandrite and Nd:YAG for hair and pigment, pulsed dye for blood vessels, and picosecond pulses for pigment and tattoos. Registered studies name its products, including a 1064-nm skin-tightening system and a 595 nm pulsed-dye laser. Research is device by device rather than for the brand as a whole.
quick.how: These are professional devices used in dermatology and aesthetic clinics. Most treatments are done in a series of sessions, and the right platform depends on the goal and the person's skin type.
quick.risks: Risks depend on the device and skin type and can include redness, pigment changes and burns. These are clinic-only devices, and operator choice and settings affect outcomes.

angle.text: "Candela laser" refers to a family of clinic laser platforms used for hair removal, pigment, redness and tattoos, so users pick the device that matches their concern and get clearer, smoother skin. Evidence exists per device rather than for the brand overall.

lumecca-ipl.summary: InMode's high-intensity IPL device that fades sun spots, freckles and facial redness for a more even complexion.

quick.overview:
Lumecca is an intense pulsed light (IPL) device from InMode, used in clinics to fade brown spots, freckles and facial redness for a more even complexion. IPL is not a laser; it uses broad-spectrum flashes rather than a single wavelength.

Filters select which targets absorb the light, melanin in pigment or hemoglobin in small vessels, and the heat breaks up pigment or closes small vessels, with surface cooling to protect skin. Studies naming Lumecca are small: 38 volunteers had dilated facial vessel response measured after three sessions, and a 20-patient study assessed redness reduction in rosacea after polychromatic light treatments.
quick.how: Treatment is done in a clinic, typically as a short series of sessions weeks apart. Spots often darken before flaking away. IPL is generally described as having little downtime.
quick.risks: IPL complications can include hyperpigmentation, especially on darker skin, and one manufacturer states IPL suits light to medium skin tones. Photosensitising drugs and damaged skin are contraindications. It is a professional device.

angle.text: Lumecca flashes broad-spectrum light that targets pigment and redness, fading sun spots, freckles and vessels for a more even facial tone. It is an IPL rather than a laser, and supporting studies are small, though IPL is an established category.

sciton-bbl-moxi-halo.summary: Sciton's IPL, light fractional 1927-nm laser and hybrid fractional laser, often combined for pigment, redness, texture and a more even complexion.

quick.overview:
BBL, Moxi and Halo are treatments on Sciton platforms: broadband light, a light fractional 1927-nm laser and a deeper hybrid fractional laser. Clinics sometimes combine them in a session to address sun damage, pigment, redness, texture and scars for a fresher, more even complexion.

BBL uses filtered flashlamp light on pigment and vessels. Moxi and Halo create tiny columns of controlled injury so skin renews and remodels. Published work naming them is small: a completed 15-person pilot combined BBL, Moxi and Halo for pigment, and a 2023 study examined fractionated 1927-nm laser for diffuse pigmentation and actinic changes.
quick.how: These are clinic procedures, often chosen in combination, with the depth set by the provider. Light settings carry short recovery, while deeper Halo settings mean more healing time. Results build over weeks as skin renews.
quick.risks: Listed concerns include pigment change after laser, healing time with deeper resurfacing, and that these are clinic-only procedures. Darker skin carries higher pigment-change risk.

angle.text: BBL clears pigment and redness with light, while Moxi and Halo resurface with fractional laser, leaving a smoother, more even complexion. People combine them for sun damage, texture and scars, and supporting studies are small pilots.

moxi-laser.summary: Sciton's light fractional 1927-nm laser for brown spots, sun damage and texture, with lighter downtime than deeper resurfacing.

quick.overview:
Moxi is a light fractional laser on the Sciton platform that works at 1927 nm. People use it for brown spots, sun damage and skin texture, seeking brighter, more even skin with lighter downtime than ablative resurfacing.

It treats a pattern of microscopic zones of skin, which are replaced during healing, leaving skin between them intact. A 2023 study examined a fractionated 1927-nm laser for diffuse dyspigmentation and actinic changes, and two completed registered studies tested the wavelength for diffuse pigmentation (30 participants) and hyperpigmentation in Fitzpatrick skin types V and VI (15 participants).
quick.how: It is a clinic procedure, usually done in a series of sessions. Skin typically looks pink and feels rough for a few days as treated zones shed. People often schedule it around sun avoidance.
quick.risks: Registry entries do not summarise adverse effects. Pigment changes are a general concern with lasers, particularly in darker skin. It is a clinic-only procedure.

angle.text: Moxi's 1927-nm fractional laser clears surface pigment and renews texture with lighter downtime, leaving brighter, more even skin. It is used for pigmentation and sun damage, and registered studies of 15 to 30 participants exist.

excel-v-laser.summary: Cutera's green 532 nm plus 1064 nm clinic laser that reduces facial redness, visible vessels and sun spots.

quick.overview:
Excel V is a Cutera clinic laser that pairs a green 532-nm wavelength with an infrared 1064-nm wavelength. People use it to reduce facial redness, small visible blood vessels, port-wine stains and brown spots for a clearer, more even face.

Green light is absorbed by blood and pigment, and the 1064-nm light reaches deeper vessels. Heat closes small vessels or breaks up pigment. Studies naming it are small: a prospective study in 5 adults for port-wine stains, a randomised study comparing 532-nm KTP and 595-nm pulsed dye lasers for red surgical scars, and registered studies in rosacea, hand lentigines and poikiloderma of Civatte.
quick.how: It is done in a clinic, usually in a short series of sessions. The provider selects the wavelength for the target, vessels or pigment. Treated areas may look red or darker for a short period before settling.
quick.risks: Registry entries reviewed do not summarise adverse effects. Vascular lasers in general may cause bruising or pigment change. It is a clinic-only device.

angle.text: Excel V's green and 1064-nm light is absorbed by vessels and pigment, closing small vessels and breaking up spots for less redness and a more even tone. It is used for rosacea, visible vessels and lentigines, and supporting studies are small.

laser-genesis.summary: A gentle low-energy 1064-nm laser facial promoted for calmer redness, even tone and fine texture with little downtime.

quick.overview:
Laser Genesis is a brand name for a low-energy 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser treatment that clinics offer for skin tone, redness and fine lines. It is usually described as a gentle option with little downtime.

The infrared light passes through the surface and warms the dermis without removing the epidermis; providers say this prompts collagen remodeling and less visible redness. Published research on it for appearance is sparse: one randomized split-face trial in eight people compared it with grid fractional radiofrequency for wrinkles around the eyes, and other registered studies are small.
quick.how: It is done in a clinic, usually as a series of sessions spaced weeks apart, with people returning to normal activity right away. Results are described as gradual improvements in tone and texture.
quick.risks: Nd:YAG lasers at 1064 nm carry an eye-injury hazard because the beam is invisible, so eye protection is used. Cosmetic adverse-event rates for this specific treatment were not found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Laser Genesis warms the dermis with a gentle 1064-nm laser, which providers say calms redness and refines texture for smoother, more even skin with little downtime. Published appearance data are limited to a small split-face trial and registered studies.

vbeam-perfecta.summary: Candela's 595 nm pulsed dye laser, a clinic mainstay for facial redness, broken capillaries and vascular lesions.

quick.overview:
Vbeam Perfecta is a pulsed dye laser from Candela used by dermatologists for port-wine stains, hemangiomas, broken capillaries and persistent facial redness. People seek it for a calmer, more even complexion, and some practices offer it for scars.

The 595 nm light is absorbed by hemoglobin, heating and closing small vessels, while a cryogen spray cools the skin surface during each pulse. Pulsed dye lasers have long been treated in the medical literature as the standard approach for port-wine stains. Studies of it for general appearance, such as photoaging, are small.
quick.how: It is done in a clinic, usually as a series of sessions weeks apart. Settings can be chosen to reduce bruising, and treated redness fades over the following days to weeks. Results build across sessions.
quick.risks: Bruising (purpura) and temporary redness or swelling are recognized effects; settings such as pulse stacking have been studied to reduce purpura. People often plan around visible marks for a period after treatment.

angle.text: Vbeam's 595-nm light is absorbed by blood, closing visible vessels and reducing facial redness for a calmer complexion. It is used for broken capillaries, rosacea-related flushing and some scars, and is well established for vascular lesions.

morpheus8-burst.summary: The deeper Burst-mode setting of InMode's Morpheus8 RF microneedling, promoted for tighter skin and mild fat remodeling around the lower face and neck.

quick.overview:
Morpheus8 Burst is the Burst-mode, deeper-reaching configuration of InMode's RF microneedling device. It is marketed for firmer skin, better texture and mild fat reduction, particularly around the lower face, jawline and neck.

Insulated needles penetrate the skin and release radiofrequency energy at chosen depths, heating tissue to prompt collagen remodeling. Research on the Burst mode specifically is minimal; one registered trial looked at multi-depth RF microneedling for cellulite.
quick.how: It is a clinic treatment, usually done as a series of sessions weeks apart, with results said to build gradually as collagen remodels. Treatment depth is set by the provider for the area.
quick.risks: Redness, swelling and pinpoint bleeding are common after treatment. Burns, scarring, infection and pigment changes are described as rarer risks. It is a clinic-only procedure.

angle.text: Burst mode sends RF energy deeper into the skin to prompt collagen remodeling and mild fat reduction, aiming for firmer skin and a tighter jawline. It is promoted for the lower face and neck, with minimal published research on this setting.

morpheus8-body.summary: InMode's RF microneedling for the abdomen, arms and thighs, used to tighten and smooth body skin, for example after weight loss.

quick.overview:
Morpheus8 Body applies InMode's RF microneedling to the abdomen, arms, thighs and other areas, marketed for tighter, smoother skin, for instance after weight loss.

Insulated needles deliver radiofrequency energy to the dermis and deeper tissue, which providers say prompts collagen remodeling. A 2024 plastic-surgery review lists Morpheus8 and Morpheus8 Body among RF-based minimally invasive tools used alongside surgical body contouring, and a registered 48-person study examined RF microneedling for leg cellulite.
quick.how: It is a clinic treatment, typically done in a series of sessions, and sometimes used alongside body contouring. Results are said to develop over weeks to months as collagen remodels.
quick.risks: Temporary redness and swelling are common; burns, scarring and infection are described as rarer risks. Independent long-term data are limited.

angle.text: Morpheus8 Body delivers RF energy into the skin of the abdomen, arms and thighs to prompt collagen remodeling, aiming for tighter, smoother body skin after weight loss. A 48-person registered study looked at RF microneedling for leg cellulite.

fractora-rf.summary: InMode's fractional RF pin handpiece, the forerunner of Morpheus8, used for skin tightening, softer acne scars and oil control.

quick.overview:
Fractora is a fractional radiofrequency handpiece from InMode, used in clinics for skin tightening, acne scars and oil production. Morpheus8 was later modified from this platform.

Arrays of pins deliver bipolar RF energy into the skin in a fractional pattern, heating tissue to prompt collagen remodeling. Studies are small prospective and retrospective ones, some combining Fractora with other RF treatments such as FaceTite, plus a sebum trial.
quick.how: It is a clinic treatment, done in a series of sessions and sometimes combined with other RF devices. Results are described as gradual as skin remodels.
quick.risks: Redness, swelling and pinpoint bleeding are commonly reported for RF microneedling. Fractora-specific adverse data were limited in the sources, and it is a clinic-only procedure.

angle.text: Fractora sends fractional RF through pins into the skin, prompting collagen remodeling and less oil for tighter skin and softer acne scars. It preceded Morpheus8 and has been studied in small, mostly early studies.
